title: Catalan grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is central Catalan, as it is spoken in Barcelona, in the current spelling.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Catalan conversation.
lessons.topic: {{em dic}} and {{et dius}}; {{soc}}, {{ets}}, {{és}} “I am, you are, he or she is”; {{de}} “from”

goal.t: Hola, em dic Laura. Soc de Boston.
goal.tr: Hi, my name's Laura. I'm from Boston.

dialog.t: Hola, Marc. Jo em dic Laura.
Jo soc d'aquí, de Barcelona. Encantat!
dialog.tr: I'm from here, from Barcelona. Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: **Saying your name.** Catalans say {{em dic}}, word for word “I call myself”: {{Em dic Laura.}} “My name's Laura.” To ask, {{Com et dius?}} “What's your name?”, word for word “how do you call yourself?”. The little words {{em}} “myself” and {{et}} “yourself” go before the verb. You'll meet many more little words like them: they are one of the things that make Catalan Catalan.

blocks.means: a word for doing or being: go, eat, live, call, be.

blocks.p: **I'm, you're.** “To be” is {{ser}}: {{soc}} “I am”, {{ets}} “you are”, {{és}} “he is, she is”. There is no word for “I” in {{Soc de Boston}}: the verb's ending already says who it is, so Catalan usually leaves “I” and “you” out. You add {{jo}} “I” or {{tu}} “you” only for a contrast: {{Jo soc d'aquí.}} “I'm from here (and you aren't).”

table: {{Ets de Barcelona?}} Are you from Barcelona?

blocks.p: **Where from.** {{de}} is “from” (and “of”). Before a vowel it becomes {{d'}}: {{D'on ets?}} “Where are you from?”, word for word “from where are you?”. The “from” always goes first, never at the end. {{I tu?}} “And you?” turns any question back to the other person.

ex.note: many cities have a Catalan name: {{Londres}}, {{Nova York}}
a question just by raising your voice at the end
{{és}} is both “he is” and “she is”: the conversation tells you who
the same for a man or a woman

blocks.tip: {{Encantat}} is said by a man, {{encantada}} by a woman: Catalan words often take an {{-a}} for a woman (lesson 3). Greetings: {{Bon dia}} “good morning” (until lunch), {{Bona tarda}} “good afternoon, good evening”, {{Bona nit}} “good night”, {{Adeu}} “bye”, {{Fins després}} “see you later”.

mistakes.why: “From” goes in front of “where”, never at the end: {{d'on}}.
{{de}} becomes {{d'}} before a vowel.

lessons.title: Order in a café
lessons.summary: Ask for what you'd like in a café or a shop, politely: “I'd like a coffee with milk, please.”
lessons.topic: {{vull}} and {{voldria}} + a thing; {{un}} and {{una}} “a”; no word for “some”; {{no}}

goal.t: Voldria un cafè amb llet, si us plau.
goal.tr: I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

dialog.tr: Good morning! What can I get you?

dialog.t: Bon dia. Voldria un cafè amb llet, si us plau.
dialog.tr: Good morning. I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

dialog.t: Sí, un croissant. I una aigua.
dialog.tr: Yes, a croissant. And a water.

blocks.p: **Asking for something.** {{Voldria}} “I'd like” is the polite way, good anywhere. {{Vull}} “I want” is fine too, with {{si us plau}} “please”: {{Vull un tallat, si us plau.}} “A cortado, please.” Then say thanks: {{gràcies}}, or {{moltes gràcies}} “thank you very much”.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or a place: coffee, waiter, Barcelona.

blocks.p: **A, an.** Catalan has two words for “a”: {{un}} and {{una}}. Every noun is either masculine or feminine (lesson 4 explains), and “a” matches it: {{un cafè}} “a coffee”, but {{una aigua}} “a water”, {{una cervesa}} “a beer”. Nouns ending in {{-a}} nearly always take {{una}}; learn the others with their {{un}} or {{una}}.

table: {{un suc de taronja}} an orange juice
{{una ampolla de vi}} a bottle of wine

blocks.p: **No word for “some”.** For things you don't count, like bread, milk or water, Catalan uses the noun alone: {{Vull pa.}} “I'd like some bread.” {{Tens llet?}} “Do you have any milk?”.
**Not.** {{no}} goes right before the verb: {{No vull sucre.}} “I don't want sugar.”

ex.t: Vull un entrepà de pernil, si us plau.
ex.tr: I'd like a ham sandwich, please.
I'd like a bottle of water.

ex.t: Un tallat i un croissant, si us plau.
ex.tr: A cortado and a croissant, please.
ex.note: {{tallat}}: an espresso with a little milk
word for word “will you charge me?”: what people say at the bar

blocks.tip: In a bar in Barcelona you'll hear {{Em poses un cafè?}} “Can I have a coffee?” (word for word “will you put me a coffee?”), and the waiter asks {{Què et poso?}} “What can I get you?”. {{em}} “(to) me” and {{et}} “(to) you” are the little words from lesson 1 again.

For things you don't count, “some” is no word at all: just {{llet}}.
{{no}} goes before the verb.

lessons.title: Say who people are and what they're like
lessons.summary: Introduce your friends and describe people: “Jordi and I are friends. He's from Girona, and he's very nice.”
lessons.topic: {{ser}} “to be” for everyone; {{jo, tu, ell, ella…}}; adjectives for a man, a woman, and more than one; {{en}} and {{la}} before names

goal.t: En Jordi i jo som amics. És de Girona i és molt simpàtic.
goal.tr: Jordi and I are friends. He's from Girona, and he's very nice.

dialog.t: Qui és la noia de la foto?
dialog.tr: Who's the girl in the photo?

dialog.t: És la Clara. És de Tarragona.
És molt simpàtica i una mica tímida.
dialog.tr: She's very nice and a little shy.

dialog.t: Són en Pere i en Joan. Són bessons!
dialog.tr: They're Pere and Joan. They're twins!

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, she, they.

blocks.p: **The whole verb.** Here is {{ser}} “to be” for everyone. The ending tells you who it is, so the pronouns are usually left out; you say them for a contrast, or when it wouldn't be clear: {{Ell és de Girona, i ella és de Vic.}} “He's from Girona, and she's from Vic.”

**{{tu}} or {{vostè}}?** {{tu}} is for friends, family, children and people your age, and it's what Catalans use most. {{vostè}} is the polite “you”, for older people and formal moments, and it takes the verb of “he, she”: {{Vostè és de Lleida?}} “Are you from Lleida?”.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: tall, nice, new.

blocks.p: **Describing a man or a woman.** Adjectives change to match the person. Most add {{-a}} for a woman: {{alt}} → {{alta}} “tall”, {{simpàtic}} → {{simpàtica}} “nice”. Many that end in {{-e}} stay the same: {{jove}} “young”, {{amable}} “kind”. For more than one, add {{-s}}, and for women change {{-a}} to {{-es}}: {{Són alts.}} “They're tall (men, or a mixed group).” {{Són altes.}} “They're tall (women).”

**Names take an article.** In everyday Catalan a name has a little word in front: {{en}} for a man, {{la}} for a woman, and {{l'}} for anyone whose name starts with a vowel: {{en Jordi}}, {{la Clara}}, {{l'Anna}}, {{l'Oriol}}. You leave it out when you speak to the person: {{Hola, Clara!}}

ex.t: En Pere i en Joan són alts.

ex.note: no word for “a” before a job

blocks.tip: {{jo}} “I” has a small letter, unlike English “I”. In Mallorca, and in some formal writing, you'll see {{na}} instead of {{la}} before a woman's name: {{na Maria}}.

mistakes.why: Clara is a woman: the adjective takes {{-a}}.
After {{ser}}, a job has no “a”: {{és professora}}.

lessons.title: Name things: “the”, “a” and more than one
lessons.summary: Name the things around you, one or many: “the keys”, “a table”, “two beers”.
lessons.topic: Masculine and feminine; {{el, la, l', els, les}} “the”; {{un, una, uns, unes}}; plurals; {{dos}}, {{dues}}

goal.t: Dos cafès i una aigua, si us plau.
goal.tr: Two coffees and a water, please.

blocks.means: whether a noun is masculine or feminine. In Catalan every noun has one, even things, and the words around it change to match.

blocks.p: **Masculine and feminine.** {{el llibre}} “the book” is masculine, {{la taula}} “the table” is feminine. There's no logic to it, but there's a strong hint: nouns ending in {{-a}} are nearly always feminine ({{la casa}} “the house”, {{la porta}} “the door”). A few aren't: {{el dia}} “the day” and {{el pa}} “the bread” are masculine. Nouns with other endings can be either: {{el cotxe}} “the car”, but {{la clau}} “the key”.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun: “the” or “a”.

blocks.p: **{{l'}}.** Before a vowel, or an {{h}} (always silent in Catalan), {{el}} and {{la}} both become {{l'}}: {{l'aigua}} “the water”, {{l'home}} “the man”. {{els}}, {{les}}, {{un}} and {{una}} never change.

blocks.means: the form of a word for more than one: books, tables. The form for one is the singular.

blocks.p: **More than one.** Most nouns add {{-s}}: {{el cotxe}} → {{els cotxes}}, {{el cafè}} → {{els cafès}}. A final {{-a}} becomes {{-es}}: {{la casa}} → {{les cases}}, {{la cervesa}} → {{les cerveses}}; sometimes the spelling shifts to keep the sound, as in {{amiga}} → {{amigues}}. Masculine nouns ending in {{-s}} add {{-os}}: {{el gos}} → {{els gossos}} “the dogs”. And nouns ending in a stressed vowel add {{-ns}}: {{l'entrepà}} → {{els entrepans}} “the sandwiches”.
**One and two.** “One” and “two” have a feminine: {{un cafè}}, {{una aigua}}; {{dos cafès}}, {{dues cerveses}}. From three on, numbers don't change: {{tres cafès}}, {{tres cerveses}}.

ex.t: Són uns amics de la Clara.

blocks.tip: Learn each noun with its article, {{el pa}}, {{la llet}} “the milk”, {{la nit}} “the night”: the article tells you its gender, and its gender changes the words around it.

mistakes.why: {{cervesa}} is feminine, so “two” is {{dues}}.
Before a vowel or a silent {{h}}, “the” is {{l'}}.
{{cotxe}} is masculine, so “the” in the plural is {{els}}.

practice.why: {{casa}} ends in {{-a}}: feminine, {{la}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.why: A final {{-a}} becomes {{-es}} in the plural: {{cerveses}}.

practice.why: Before a vowel, {{la}} becomes {{l'}}.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask who, what, where, when, how and why, and ask yes-or-no questions just with your voice.
lessons.topic: Question words: {{què, qui, on, quan, com, per què, quant, quin}}; questions by intonation; {{oi?}}

goal.tr: Where do you live? And what do you do?

dialog.tr: And what are you doing in Barcelona?

dialog.t: Estudio a la universitat. I tu, on vius?
dialog.tr: I'm studying at the university. And you, where do you live?

blocks.p: **Yes or no.** A yes-or-no question is the same sentence said with your voice going up: {{Ets anglès.}} “You're English.” → {{Ets anglès?}} “Are you English?”. Nothing moves, and there's no word like “do”: {{Parles català?}} “Do you speak Catalan?”. In speech you'll often hear {{que}} at the start, just to signal a question: {{Que ets anglès?}}. And {{oi?}} at the end means “right?”: {{Ets d'aquí, oi?}} “You're from here, right?”.

table: {{Per què estudies català?}} Why are you learning Catalan?
{{Quin dia és avui?}} What day is it today?

blocks.p: **The question word comes first**, then the verb, and the person (if you say who) after it: {{On viu la Marta?}} “Where does Marta live?”. A little word like “from” or “with” goes in front of the question word, never at the end: {{D'on ets?}} “Where are you from?”, {{Amb qui vius?}} “Who do you live with?”.
**Accents.** {{què}} “what” has an accent, which tells it apart from {{que}} “that”. “Why” is two words, {{per què}}, while the answer “because” is one: {{perquè}}.

blocks.tip: {{Com?}} on its own means “Sorry?”, when you didn't catch something. More polite: {{Perdona, pots repetir?}} “Sorry, can you say that again?”.

mistakes.why: A word like {{amb}} “with” goes in front of the question word, never at the end.
“What” is {{què}}, with an accent.

mistakes.wrong: Per què? Per què és tard.
mistakes.why: “Why” is {{per què}}, two words; “because” is {{perquè}}, one word.

practice.why: {{qui}} is “who”, for people.

lessons.title: Ask where things are
lessons.summary: Ask the way and say where things are: “Excuse me, where's the station? —It's next to the market.”
lessons.topic: {{ser}} for where things are: {{On és…? És a…}}; {{al}}, {{del}}, {{pel}}; place words: {{a prop de, al costat de, davant de…}}

dialog.t: Perdoni, on és l'estació de tren?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the train station?

dialog.t: És a prop, al final d'aquest carrer.
dialog.tr: It's close, at the end of this street.

dialog.t: La farmàcia és a la plaça, davant de l'església.
dialog.tr: The pharmacy is on the square, across from the church.

blocks.p: **Where, with {{ser}}.** To say where something is, Catalan uses {{ser}}, the verb of {{soc de Boston}}: {{On és l'estació?}} “Where's the station?” {{És a la plaça.}} “It's on the square.” For people you'll hear both {{ser}} and {{estar}} (lesson 9): {{Soc a casa}} and {{Estic a casa}} both mean “I'm at home”.

blocks.means: a little word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to say where: in, at, from, next to.

blocks.p: **{{a}} “in, at, to”.** {{a}} is the all-purpose word for places: {{a Barcelona}} “in Barcelona”, {{a la plaça}} “on the square”, {{a casa}} “at home”. With {{el}} it joins into one word: {{a}} + {{el}} = {{al}}: {{al mercat}} “at the market”. {{de}} and {{per}} “through, around” do the same. With {{la}} and {{l'}} nothing joins: {{a la plaça}}, {{de l'església}}.

table: on the right, on the left

ex.t: On és el lavabo, si us plau?
És a la dreta, al costat de la porta.
ex.tr: It's on the right, next to the door.

ex.t: El museu és a prop del port.
ex.tr: The museum is near the harbor.
The hotel is across from the station.
Is the beach far from here?

blocks.tip: {{Perdoni}} “excuse me” is polite, for a stranger you'd call {{vostè}}; {{Perdona}} is for someone you call {{tu}}. The answer to {{gràcies}} is {{de res}} “you're welcome”.

mistakes.wrong: El museu és a prop el port.
mistakes.right: El museu és a prop del port.
mistakes.tr: The museum is near the harbor.
mistakes.why: {{a prop}} “near” needs {{de}}, and {{de}} + {{el}} becomes {{del}}.
{{a}} + {{el}} always joins into {{al}}.

lessons.title: Say what there is
lessons.summary: Ask if there's a pharmacy nearby, and say what there is and isn't: “Is there a cash machine near here?”
lessons.topic: {{hi ha}} “there is, there are”; {{no hi ha}}, {{no hi ha cap}}; {{hi ha}} or {{és}}

goal.t: Hi ha una farmàcia a prop d'aquí?
goal.tr: Is there a pharmacy near here?

dialog.tr: Is there wifi in the room?

dialog.t: Sí, i la contrasenya és a la targeta.
dialog.tr: Yes, and the password is on the card.

dialog.t: I hi ha un supermercat a prop?
dialog.tr: And is there a supermarket nearby?

dialog.t: Sí, n'hi ha un aquí al costat.
dialog.tr: Yes, there's one right next door.

dialog.t: Sí, de set a deu, al menjador.
dialog.tr: Yes, from seven to ten, in the dining room.

blocks.p: **{{hi ha}}** means both “there is” and “there are”: it never changes for the plural. {{Hi ha un bar.}} “There's a bar.” {{Hi ha dos bars.}} “There are two bars.” To ask, just raise your voice: {{Hi ha un bar a prop?}} “Is there a bar nearby?” For “there isn't”, put {{no}} in front: {{No hi ha pa.}} “There's no bread.” And with things you count, “no” is {{cap}}: {{No hi ha cap farmàcia.}} “There's no pharmacy.”

**The {{hi}}** is a little word meaning “there”, from the same family as {{em}} and {{et}}. In this phrase it always comes with {{ha}}, so learn {{hi ha}} as one block. You'll meet {{hi}} on its own in lesson 26.

**{{hi ha}} or {{és}}?** Use {{hi ha}} to say that something exists somewhere, usually with “a”, a number or nothing: {{Hi ha una farmàcia a la plaça.}} “There's a pharmacy on the square.” Use {{és}} to say where a particular thing is, with “the”: {{La farmàcia és a la plaça.}} “The pharmacy is on the square.”

table: The cash machine is at the entrance.

ex.t: Hi ha un caixer a prop d'aquí?
ex.tr: Is there a cash machine near here?

ex.t: A la plaça hi ha un mercat molt bonic.
ex.tr: There's a really nice market on the square.

ex.note: word for word “what is there for dinner?”

ex.t: N'hi ha un aquí al costat.
ex.note: {{n'hi ha un}} “there is one (of them)”: lesson 23 explains the {{n'}}

blocks.tip: {{hi ha}} comes from the verb {{haver}}. In the past it becomes {{hi havia}} “there was, there were” (lesson 30).

mistakes.why: {{hi ha}} doesn't change for the plural.

mistakes.wrong: Hi ha la farmàcia a la plaça.
mistakes.right: La farmàcia és a la plaça.
mistakes.tr: The pharmacy is on the square.

{{no}} goes first, then {{hi ha}}, together.

lessons.title: Point, choose and pay in a shop
lessons.summary: Point at what you want, ask how much it is, and understand the price: “How much are these oranges?”

dialog.tr: Good morning! What can I get you?

dialog.t: Bon dia. Quant costen aquestes taronges?
dialog.tr: Good morning. How much are these oranges?

dialog.t: Doncs un quilo, si us plau. I aquells tomàquets?
dialog.tr: A kilo, then, please. And those tomatoes?
OK, half a kilo. How much is that?

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{aquest}} is “this” (near you), {{aquell}} is “that” (over there). Like adjectives, they match the noun:
**{{això}} and {{allò}}** are “this” and “that” for something you don't name, or don't know the name of: {{Què és això?}} “What's this?” {{Quant costa això?}} “How much is this?”. They never change.

**Which one?** {{quin}} (feminine {{quina}}, plural {{quins}}, {{quines}}): {{Quin vols?}} “Which one do you want?” {{Aquest, si us plau.}} “This one, please.” On its own, {{aquest}} means “this one”.

**How much.** {{Quant costa?}} for one thing, {{Quant costen?}} for several. When you pay: {{Quant és?}} “How much is it (all)?”. Prices: {{dos euros amb cinquanta}} “two fifty” (€2.50), {{cinquanta cèntims}} “fifty cents”.

From 21 to 29 the numbers are joined with {{-i-}}: {{vint-i-u}}, {{vint-i-dos}}, {{vint-i-cinc}}. From 31 on, just a hyphen: {{trenta-u}}, {{quaranta-dos}}, {{setanta-cinc}}. When counting you say {{u}}; before a noun, {{un}} or {{una}}: {{vint-i-una cerveses}}.

ex.t: Quina vols, la vermella o la blava?
ex.tr: Which one do you want, the red one or the blue one?
ex.note: {{la vermella}} “the red one”: just the article and the adjective

blocks.tip: Paying: {{Puc pagar amb targeta?}} “Can I pay by card?”, or {{en efectiu}} “in cash”. In a shop you'll hear {{Alguna cosa més?}} “Anything else?”, and you answer {{Res més, gràcies}} “Nothing else, thanks”.

{{taronja}} is feminine: {{aquesta}}.
For a thing you don't name, “this” is {{això}}.

lessons.title: Say how you are and how things are
lessons.summary: Ask how someone is, say how you feel today, and tell apart what something is from how it is right now.
lessons.topic: {{estar}} for how you are: {{estic, estàs, està…}}; {{ser}} or {{estar}}

goal.t: Estic una mica cansada, però estic bé.
goal.tr: I'm a bit tired, but I'm fine.
goal.note: said by a woman; a man says {{cansat}}

dialog.t: Bé, gràcies. Una mica cansada. I tu?
dialog.tr: Fine, thanks. A bit tired. And you?

dialog.t: Molt bé! Estic molt content: avui és divendres!
dialog.tr: Great! I'm really happy: it's Friday today!

blocks.p: **{{estar}}** is the other “to be”. It's for how someone or something is at the moment: how you feel, a state that comes and goes.

**{{ser}} or {{estar}}?** {{ser}} says what someone or something is: who, what kind, where from, what they're like. {{estar}} says how they are right now. Compare {{És avorrit.}} “He's boring.” with {{Està avorrit.}} “He's bored.”

table: {{La Marta és alegre.}} Marta is a cheerful person.
{{La Marta està contenta.}} Marta is happy (right now).
{{En Pau és de Vic.}} Pau is from Vic.
{{En Pau està malalt.}} Pau is sick.
{{La sopa és bona.}} The soup is good.
{{La sopa està freda.}} The soup is cold.

blocks.tip: {{Com estàs?}} is for a friend; to someone you call {{vostè}}: {{Com està?}}. Quick and friendly: {{Com va?}} “How's it going?”, answered {{Bé!}}, {{Molt bé!}} or {{Tirant}}.

mistakes.why: Being tired comes and goes: {{estar}}.
Where someone is from is part of who they are: {{ser}}.

lessons.title: Say what you have, your age, and when you're hungry
lessons.summary: Say what you have and don't have, how old you are, and that you're hungry, thirsty or cold: “I'm twenty-five, and I'm really hungry!”
lessons.topic: {{tenir}} “to have”: {{tinc, tens, té…}}; {{tinc 25 anys}}; {{tinc gana, set, son, fred, calor}}

goal.t: Tinc vint-i-cinc anys i tinc molta gana!
goal.tr: I'm twenty-five, and I'm really hungry!

dialog.tr: Phew, it's so hot! Are you thirsty?

dialog.t: Tinc aigua i dos entrepans. Vols?
dialog.tr: I have water and two sandwiches. Do you want some?

blocks.p: **{{tenir}}** “to have”:

{{Tinc un germà.}} “I have a brother.” {{No tinc cotxe.}} “I don't have a car.” In questions and after {{no}}, something you'd normally have just one of goes without “a”: {{Tens cotxe?}} “Do you have a car?”, {{No tinc temps.}} “I don't have time.”
**Age with {{tenir}}.** In Catalan you “have” your years: {{Tinc trenta anys.}} “I'm thirty.” {{Quants anys tens?}} “How old are you?”, word for word “how many years do you have?”.

**Hungry, thirsty, cold: you “have” them too.** {{Tinc gana.}} “I'm hungry.” {{Tinc set.}} “I'm thirsty.” {{Tinc son.}} “I'm sleepy.” {{Tinc fred.}} “I'm cold.” {{Tinc calor.}} “I'm hot.” {{Tinc pressa.}} “I'm in a hurry.” {{Tinc por.}} “I'm scared.” They're nouns, so “very” is “a lot of”: {{Tinc molta gana}}, {{molta set}}, {{molta calor}}; with {{fred}}, {{molt de fred}}.

ex.tr: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

blocks.tip: {{té}} “has” keeps its accent: without it, {{te}} is “tea”.

mistakes.why: Age goes with {{tenir}}: “I have twenty years”.
Feeling cold is something you “have”: {{tinc fred}}. A cold thing takes {{estar}}: {{El cafè està fred.}} “The coffee is cold.”
{{gana}} is a feminine noun, so “a lot of” is {{molta}}.

lessons.title: Talk about your family
lessons.summary: Say who's who in your family, and ask about someone else's: “My sister's name is Anna, and she has two kids.”
lessons.topic: {{el meu, la meva…}} “my”, {{el teu}} “your”, {{el seu}} “his, her, their”: possessives with the article

goal.t: La meva germana es diu Anna i té dos fills.
goal.tr: My sister's name is Anna, and she has two kids.

dialog.t: Sí! Aquests són els meus pares, i aquest és el meu germà petit.
dialog.tr: Yes! These are my parents, and this is my little brother.

dialog.t: És la meva germana. Es diu Anna i té dos fills.
dialog.tr: That's my sister. Her name's Anna, and she has two kids.

dialog.t: El seu marit és en Mark. És de Texas.
dialog.tr: Her husband is Mark. He's from Texas.

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, our.

blocks.p: **My, your… with “the”.** In Catalan, “my” comes with the article: {{el meu germà}}, word for word “the my brother”. And it matches the thing owned, not the owner: {{el meu pare}} “my father”, {{la meva mare}} “my mother”, {{els meus pares}} “my parents”, {{les meves amigues}} “my (female) friends”.

**His or her?** {{el seu}} is “his”, “her”, “their” and the polite “your”. It matches the thing, never the owner: {{la seva mare}} can be “his mother” or “her mother”, and the conversation makes it clear. Kate's sister's husband is {{el seu marit}}, masculine, because {{marit}} is.
**Names.** {{Es diu Anna}} “her name is Anna”: after {{em dic}} and {{et dius}} (lesson 1), {{es diu}} is the form for “he, she”.
As with {{germans}}, the masculine plural covers a mixed group: {{els pares}} “mother and father”, {{els fills}} “sons and daughters”, {{els avis}} “grandparents”.

ex.t: Els meus avis viuen a Reus.
Com es diu la teva parella?
La nostra filla té sis anys.
En Joan i la seva dona són molt simpàtics.
ex.tr: Joan and his wife are very nice.

ex.note: {{casa meva}} “my home”: with {{casa}}, the possessive goes after it, with no article

blocks.tip: The possessive can also follow the noun: {{un amic meu}} “a friend of mine”, {{una cosina meva}} “a cousin of mine”.

mistakes.why: “My” comes with the article: {{el meu}}.

mistakes.wrong: El meva mare és de Lleida.
mistakes.right: La meva mare és de Lleida.
mistakes.why: {{mare}} is feminine: {{la meva}}.

mistakes.wrong: La Kate és aquí amb la seva marit.
mistakes.right: La Kate és aquí amb el seu marit.
mistakes.tr: Kate is here with her husband.
mistakes.why: The possessive matches the husband (masculine), not Kate: {{el seu marit}} “her husband”.
